modules.title: The Basics
modules.desc: Start here: teams, the ground, the kit and how runs are scored.

cards.title: Two teams, eleven players
body: Cricket is played by **two teams** of **11 players** each.
One team **bats** and tries to score runs. The other team **bowls and fields** and tries to stop them.
The team that is bowling and fielding is called the **fielding side**.
Only **two batters** from the batting side are on the field at a time.
cards.fact: There is always one batter at each end of the pitch.

cards.title: What is an innings?
body: An **innings** is one team's turn to bat.
An innings ends when **10 batters are out** (the last batter has no partner left), or when the overs run out, or when the captain **declares**.
Then the teams swap: the batting side fields and the fielding side bats.
That is why a team of 11 is **all out** after only 10 wickets.
cards.fact: A captain can declare an innings closed in Test cricket to give the bowlers more time to win.

cards.title: The aim of the game
body: The aim is simple: **score more runs than the other team**.
Batters score **runs** by running between the wickets or hitting the ball to the boundary.
Bowlers and fielders try to get batters **out** and stop runs being scored.
Getting a batter out is called taking a **wicket**.

cards.title: How a team wins
body: If the team that **bats first** wins, they win **by runs**. Example: they score 200, the other team scores 180 — they win **by 20 runs**.
If the team that **bats second** (the chasing team) passes the target, they win **by wickets** — the number of wickets they still had left.
Example: chasing 200, a team reaches 201 having lost 4 wickets — they win **by 6 wickets**.
If both teams score exactly the same, it is a **tie**.
cards.fact: In Test cricket, if time runs out before a result, the match is a **draw**.

cards.title: The toss
body: Before the match, the two **captains** meet for the **toss**.
A coin is flipped. One captain calls **heads** or **tails**.
The captain who wins the toss chooses whether their team will **bat first** or **bowl first**.
Captains think about the pitch, the weather and their team before choosing.

cards.title: Three main formats
body: **Test cricket**: the longest format, played over up to **5 days**. Each team gets **two innings**.
**ODI** (One Day International): each team bats for up to **50 overs**.
**T20** (Twenty20): each team bats for up to **20 overs** — fast and exciting!
An **over** is a set of **6 legal balls** bowled by one bowler.
cards.fact: A T20 match usually finishes in about three to four hours, while a Test can last five days.

quiz.q: How many players are in a cricket team?
quiz.ex: Each cricket team has 11 players.

quiz.q: How many batters from the batting side are on the field at the same time?
quiz.ex: Only two batters are out in the middle at a time, one at each end.

quiz.q: Why is a team 'all out' after only 10 wickets?
options: Because the last batter has no partner left to bat with
Because 10 is the maximum in the rules for every format
quiz.ex: Batting needs two batters. After 10 are out, the last one is left alone, so the innings ends.

quiz.q: Team A bats first and scores 250. Team B scores 230. What is the result?
quiz.ex: The team batting first wins by the difference in runs: 250 − 230 = 20 runs.

quiz.q: Chasing 180, a team reaches 181 after losing 3 wickets. They win by…
quiz.ex: A chasing team wins by the wickets it still had left: 10 − 3 = 7 wickets.

quiz.q: What does the captain who wins the toss decide?
options: Whether to bat or bowl first
quiz.ex: The toss winner chooses whether their team bats first or bowls first.

quiz.q: In a T20 match, each team bats for up to how many overs?
quiz.ex: T20 means Twenty20 — up to 20 overs per side. ODIs are 50 overs.

quiz.q: In Test cricket, each team gets two innings.
quiz.ex: True. A Test is played over up to 5 days and each team can bat twice.

cards.title: The cricket ground
body: A cricket ground is a big oval or round field.
The edge of the field is marked by the **boundary** — often a rope.
Right in the middle is the **pitch**, where the bowling and batting happen.
Fielders stand in different **positions** all around the ground.

cards.title: The 30-yard circle
body: Around the pitch there is a marked ring called the **30-yard circle** or **inner ring**.
It matters in **ODI** and **T20** cricket: there are limits on how many fielders may stand **outside** it.
Fielders inside the circle save singles. Fielders outside it stop boundaries.
You will learn the exact fielding limits in the **Laws of the Game** module.

cards.title: The pitch
body: The pitch is a strip of short, hard grass and earth in the middle.
It is **22 yards (20.12 m)** long between the two sets of stumps.
It is **10 feet (3.05 m)** wide.
Players try not to run on the middle of the pitch, so it is not damaged.
cards.fact: 22 yards is also called one **chain** — an old unit of length!

cards.title: Stumps and bails
body: At each end of the pitch stands a **wicket**: **three stumps** with **two bails** resting on top.
The stumps are **28 inches (71.1 cm)** high.
The whole wicket is **9 inches (22.86 cm)** wide.
The wicket is **broken** when a bail falls off or a stump is knocked out of the ground.

cards.title: The creases
body: White lines painted on the pitch are called **creases**.
The **bowling crease** is the line the stumps stand on.
The **popping crease** is **4 feet (1.22 m)** in front of the bowling crease. The batter stands near it.
The **return creases** run at right angles from the popping crease on each side, marking where the bowler's back foot must land.

cards.title: Making your ground
body: A batter is **in their ground** when their **bat** (held in the hand) or some part of their **body** is grounded **behind the popping crease**.
**On the line is not in!** The line belongs to the fielding side, so you must be behind it.
A batter **out of their ground** can be **run out** or **stumped** if the wicket is broken.
When running, always **slide your bat** over the line to make your ground safely.
cards.fact: Sliding your bat in is faster than running all the way in yourself — it reaches the line first.

quiz.q: How long is a cricket pitch, from one set of stumps to the other?
quiz.ex: The pitch is 22 yards (20.12 m) long.

quiz.q: How wide is the pitch?
quiz.ex: The pitch is 10 feet (3.05 m) wide.

quiz.q: How many stumps and bails make up one wicket?
quiz.ex: A wicket is three stumps with two bails resting on top.

quiz.q: How far in front of the bowling crease is the popping crease?
quiz.ex: The popping crease is 4 feet (1.22 m) in front of the bowling crease.

quiz.q: A batter's bat is resting exactly ON the popping crease line, not behind it. Are they in their ground?
options: No — on the line is not in
Yes — the line counts as in
Only if the umpire is not looking
quiz.ex: You must be grounded behind the popping crease. The line itself does not count as in.

quiz.q: What is the ring marked around the pitch, used in ODI and T20 fielding rules?
quiz.ex: The 30-yard circle (inner ring) limits how many fielders may stand outside it in limited-overs cricket.

quiz.q: Look at the picture. Which fielding position is marked, standing right behind the batter's stumps?
quiz.ex: The wicket-keeper crouches behind the stumps at the batter's end.

quiz.q: The wicket is 'broken' when a bail falls off or a stump is knocked out of the ground.
quiz.ex: True. The wicket must be broken for a batter to be bowled, run out or stumped.

cards.title: The cricket ball
body: A cricket ball is hard. It has a **cork** centre wrapped in string and covered in **leather**.
Around the middle is a raised, stitched **seam**. Bowlers use it to make the ball move.
A men's ball weighs **155.9–163 g** and is **22.4–22.9 cm** around.
cards.fact: Because the ball is so hard, safety equipment is very important.

cards.title: Red, white and pink
body: **Red ball**: used in **Test** and first-class cricket played in white clothes.
**White ball**: used in **ODI** and **T20** cricket, where teams wear coloured clothes.
**Pink ball**: used in **day-night Test** matches, because it is easier to see under floodlights.

cards.title: The bat
body: Cricket bats are made of **willow** wood.
A bat can be at most **38 inches (96.52 cm)** long.
It can be at most **4.25 inches (10.8 cm)** wide.
The flat front is the **face**, the bottom is the **toe**, and you hold the **handle**.

cards.title: Batter's protection
body: **Pads** protect the legs from the hard ball.
**Batting gloves** protect the fingers and hands.
A **helmet** with a grille protects the head and face.
An **abdominal guard** (box) protects the groin.
Many batters also wear thigh guards and arm guards.

cards.title: The wicket-keeper's kit
body: The **wicket-keeper** wears big, padded **keeping gloves** with webbing between thumb and finger.
The keeper also wears **leg pads** (keeping pads).
Only the wicket-keeper is allowed to wear gloves and external leg guards on the fielding side.
Keepers often wear a helmet when standing up close to the stumps.
cards.fact: If another fielder wore gloves, that would break the Laws!

cards.title: Stay safe
body: **Always wear a helmet** when batting against a hard ball, and when keeping up to the stumps.
Fielders very close to the bat (like **short leg**) should wear a helmet and shin guards too.
Never stand near someone swinging a bat.
Warm up before playing and drink water on hot days.

quiz.q: What is the outside of a cricket ball made of?
quiz.ex: A cricket ball has a cork centre and a leather cover with a stitched seam.

quiz.q: Which colour ball is used in day-night Test matches?
quiz.ex: The pink ball is easier to see under floodlights, so it is used for day-night Tests.

quiz.q: Which colour ball is used in ODI and T20 cricket?
quiz.ex: White balls are used in limited-overs cricket, where teams wear coloured clothing.

quiz.q: What wood are cricket bats made from?
quiz.ex: Cricket bats are made of willow.

quiz.q: What is the maximum length of a cricket bat?
quiz.ex: The Laws allow a bat up to 38 inches (96.52 cm) long.

quiz.q: What is the raised, stitched line around a cricket ball called?
quiz.ex: The seam helps bowlers move the ball.

quiz.q: A fielder at mid-on puts on a pair of gloves to stop the ball hurting. Is this allowed?
options: Yes, any fielder may wear gloves
No — only the wicket-keeper may wear gloves
quiz.ex: Only the wicket-keeper may wear gloves and external leg guards on the fielding side.

quiz.q: Which piece of equipment protects a batter's head and face?
quiz.ex: A helmet with a grille protects the head and face. Always wear one against a hard ball.

cards.title: Running between the wickets
body: After hitting the ball, both batters can **run** to the other end.
When both batters have crossed and **made their ground** at the other end, **one run** is scored.
They can turn and run again for 2, 3 or more runs.
Call clearly: **"Yes!"**, **"No!"** or **"Wait!"** — good calling stops run outs.

cards.title: The short run
body: When turning for another run, a batter must ground their bat or body **behind the popping crease**.
If they turn **short** of the crease, that run does **not count**.
The umpire calls and signals **"short run"**, and one run is taken away.
cards.fact: Always slide your bat over the line before you turn!

cards.title: Fours and sixes
body: If the ball **reaches or crosses the boundary** after bouncing or rolling, it is **4 runs**.
If the ball **crosses the boundary on the full** (without bouncing), it is **6 runs**.
If a fielder touches the ball while touching the boundary rope, it counts as a boundary too.
The batters do not need to run for a boundary.

cards.title: Overthrows
body: Sometimes a fielder's throw misses the stumps and nobody stops it.
The batters may run **extra runs** — these are called **overthrows**.
If an overthrow runs away to the boundary, the batting side gets **4** plus the runs already completed.
The run the batters were in the middle of also counts — but only if they had **crossed** when the throw was made.

cards.title: Extras
body: **Extras** are runs not scored off the bat. They go to the team's total.
**Wide**: the ball is too wide for the batter to hit. **1 run** is added.
**No-ball**: an illegal delivery, such as overstepping the crease. **1 run** is added.
**Bye**: the ball misses the bat and the batter, and the batters run.
**Leg-bye**: the ball hits the batter's body (not the bat), and the batters run — but only if the batter **tried to hit it** or **tried to get out of the way**.
cards.fact: Wides and no-balls count against the bowler. Byes and leg-byes do not.

cards.title: Reading the scoreboard
body: A score like **145/6** means **145 runs** for the loss of **6 wickets**.
**18.3 overs** means **18 complete overs and 3 balls** — not 18 and a third!
After 18.5 comes **19.0**, because an over has only 6 balls.
The **target** is one more than the other team's score.

cards.title: Run rate
body: The **run rate** is the average number of runs scored **per over**.
Run rate = **runs ÷ overs**.
Example: **120 runs in 20 overs** = **6 runs per over**.
The **required run rate** tells a chasing team how fast they must score to win.

quiz.q: When is one run completed?
options: When the batter hits the ball
When both batters have crossed and made their ground at the other end
When the bowler picks up the ball
quiz.ex: Both batters must cross and make their ground at the opposite end for a run to count.

quiz.q: The ball bounces once and then rolls over the boundary rope. How many runs?
quiz.ex: A ball that reaches the boundary after bouncing scores 4.

quiz.q: The ball flies over the boundary rope without bouncing. How many runs?
quiz.ex: Crossing the boundary on the full is a six.

quiz.q: Running two, a batter turns without grounding their bat behind the popping crease. What happens?
options: Short run — that run does not count
quiz.ex: Turning short of the crease is a short run, so one run is taken away.

quiz.q: The ball misses the bat and the batter's body, the keeper fumbles it, and the batters run one. What is this run called?
quiz.ex: A bye is when the ball misses both bat and batter and the batters run.

quiz.q: What does a score of 145/6 mean?
options: 145 runs for the loss of 6 wickets
quiz.ex: The first number is runs and the second is wickets lost.

quiz.q: A team has batted 18.3 overs. How many balls have been bowled in total?
quiz.ex: 18 overs × 6 balls = 108, plus 3 more balls = 111 balls.

quiz.q: A team scores 120 runs in 20 overs. What is its run rate?
quiz.ex: Run rate = runs ÷ overs = 120 ÷ 20 = 6 runs per over.

modules.title: Laws of the Game
modules.desc: Think like an umpire: overs, extras, every way to get out, signals and special rules.

cards.title: The over
body: An **over** is **6 legal balls** bowled by one bowler from one end.
Wides and no-balls are **not legal balls**, so they must be bowled again.
After each over, the next over is bowled from the **other end**.
A bowler may **not bowl two overs in a row** (no consecutive overs).

cards.title: No-ball: the feet
body: **Front foot**: when the front foot lands, some part of it must be **behind the popping crease**. If it is all over the line, it is a no-ball.
**Back foot**: the back foot must land **inside the return crease** without touching it.
Front-foot no-balls are the most common kind — bowlers practise their run-up to avoid them.

cards.title: No-ball: other causes
body: A **full toss above waist height** of the batter (standing upright) is a no-ball.
**Throwing** the ball: an elbow straightening by more than **15 degrees** is illegal.
More than **two fielders behind square on the leg side** at the moment of delivery (Law 28.4).
The **wicket-keeper** taking the ball **in front of the stumps** before it passes the wicket or touches the bat or batter.
A ball that **bounces more than twice** or rolls along the ground before reaching the batter.

cards.title: What a no-ball gives
body: The batting side gets **1 extra run**, and any runs hit off the bat also count.
The umpire calls **"No ball!"** and holds **one arm out sideways**.
Off a no-ball, a batter **cannot** be bowled, caught, LBW, stumped or hit wicket.
They **can** still be **run out**, or out for hitting the ball twice or obstructing the field.

cards.title: Free hit!
body: In **ICC ODIs and T20Is**, the ball after **every no-ball** is a **free hit**.
On a free hit, the batter can only be out in ways that are also possible off a no-ball — like **run out**.
So the batter can swing hard without fear of being bowled or caught!
cards.fact: If the free-hit ball is itself a wide or no-ball, the next ball is still a free hit.

cards.title: Wide
body: A **wide** is a ball so far from the batter that they could not hit it with a normal cricket shot.
The batting side gets **1 extra run**, plus any runs they take.
The umpire signals a wide by stretching **both arms out sideways**.
In ODIs and T20s umpires are strict — balls passing down the leg side are often called wide.

cards.title: Dead ball
body: When the ball is **dead**, nothing more can happen — no runs and no wickets.
The ball becomes dead when it **settles** in the keeper's or bowler's hands, crosses the **boundary**, or a batter is **out**.
An umpire can also call **dead ball**, for example if the batter was not ready.
The signal is **crossing and uncrossing the wrists** below the waist.

quiz.q: How many legal balls are in an over?
quiz.ex: An over has 6 legal balls. Wides and no-balls are bowled again.

quiz.q: Can a bowler bowl two overs in a row?
quiz.ex: A bowler may not bowl consecutive overs.

quiz.q: A bowler's front foot lands completely over the popping crease, with no part behind it. What is called?
quiz.ex: Some part of the front foot must be behind the popping crease, otherwise it is a no-ball.

quiz.q: A full toss reaches the batter above waist height. What should the umpire call?
quiz.ex: A full toss above waist height of a batter standing upright is a no-ball.

quiz.q: Look at the picture: three fielders are behind square on the leg side (not counting the keeper) when the ball is bowled. Legal?
options: No — only two are allowed, so it is a no-ball
Only if one of them is the bowler
quiz.ex: Law 28.4 allows no more than two fielders (excluding the keeper) behind square on the leg side.

quiz.q: On a free hit, the batter hits the ball straight to a fielder, who catches it. Is the batter out?
options: Not out — you cannot be caught on a free hit
quiz.ex: On a free hit you can only be out in ways possible off a no-ball, such as run out. Caught is not one of them.

quiz.q: A ball passes far outside off stump, out of the batter's reach. The umpire stretches both arms sideways. What has been called?
quiz.ex: Both arms stretched out sideways is the signal for a wide.

quiz.q: After a no-ball, a batter hits the ball for 4. How many runs does the batting side get from that delivery?
quiz.ex: 1 run for the no-ball plus the 4 runs hit off the bat = 5.

cards.title: Bowled
body: **Bowled**: the ball breaks the batter's wicket.
It is still bowled if the ball first hits the **bat** or the batter's **body** before hitting the stumps (for example an inside edge).
At least **one bail must fall** — if the ball hits the stumps but the bails stay on, it is not out!
cards.fact: Bowled is one of the most exciting sights in cricket: stumps flying!

cards.title: Caught
body: **Caught**: a fielder catches the ball off the **bat** (or the glove holding the bat) **before it touches the ground**.
The fielder must have **control** of the ball. It must not cross the boundary in their hands.
After a catch, the **new batter takes strike** — even if the batters crossed — unless it was the last ball of the over.
cards.fact: That 'new batter on strike' rule came in with the 2022 Laws update.

cards.title: Stumped
body: **Stumped**: the batter is **out of their ground**, **not trying to run**, and the **wicket-keeper** breaks the wicket.
It usually happens when a batter steps out to a spin bowler and misses the ball.
A batter **cannot** be stumped off a **no-ball**.

cards.title: Run out
body: **Run out**: while the ball is in play, a batter is **out of their ground** and a fielder breaks the wicket at that end.
Any fielder can do it — with a direct throw, or by breaking the wicket with the ball in hand.
A batter **can** be run out even off a no-ball or a wide.

cards.title: Hit wicket
body: **Hit wicket**: the batter breaks their **own wicket** with their bat or body.
This counts while playing a shot, or while setting off for the first run.
Example: a batter steps back to pull, and their back foot knocks off a bail. Out!

cards.title: Who gets the credit?
body: The **bowler** is credited with the wicket for: **bowled, caught, LBW, stumped** and **hit wicket**.
**Run outs** are **not** credited to the bowler — the fielders get the praise.
A scorecard shows it like this: "c Smith b Khan" means caught by Smith, bowled by Khan.

quiz.q: The ball hits the stumps, but neither bail falls off. Is the batter bowled?
options: Yes, hitting the stumps is enough
No — a bail must fall or a stump be knocked out
quiz.ex: The wicket must be broken: at least one bail must fall, or a stump be knocked out of the ground.

quiz.q: The ball takes an inside edge off the bat and goes on to hit the stumps. How is the batter out?
quiz.ex: It is still bowled if the ball hits the bat or body first and then breaks the wicket.

quiz.q: A fielder catches the ball, but it bounced just before reaching their hands. Out?
options: Not out — it touched the ground first
quiz.ex: For a catch, the ball must not touch the ground before the fielder takes it.

quiz.q: The striker is caught on the 3rd ball of the over, after the batters crossed. Who faces the next ball?
quiz.ex: Since 2022, the new batter takes strike after a catch, unless it was the end of the over.

quiz.q: A batter steps out to a spinner, misses, and the keeper whips off the bails. The batter was not trying to run. How are they out?
quiz.ex: Out of the ground, not attempting a run, and the keeper broke the wicket: stumped.

quiz.q: Can a batter be stumped off a no-ball?
quiz.ex: A batter cannot be stumped off a no-ball. They can still be run out.

quiz.q: Playing a pull shot, a batter's back foot knocks a bail off. What is the decision?
options: Not out — it was an accident
quiz.ex: Breaking your own wicket while playing a shot is hit wicket.

quiz.q: Which of these dismissals is NOT credited to the bowler?
quiz.ex: Bowlers get credit for bowled, caught, LBW, stumped and hit wicket — but not run outs.

cards.title: What is LBW?
body: **LBW** means **Leg Before Wicket**.
A batter can be out if the ball hits their **body** (usually the pad) when it would have gone on to **hit the stumps**.
The fielding side must **appeal** — usually by shouting **"Howzat?"** — and the bowler's-end umpire decides.
LBW has several conditions. **All** must be true for it to be out.

cards.title: Step 1: Legal ball, no bat first
body: The delivery must **not** be a **no-ball**.
The ball must **not** hit the **bat** (or the glove holding the bat) **first**.
If the ball hits the bat first and then the pad, it is **not out LBW**.

cards.title: Step 2: Where did it pitch?
body: Look at where the ball **bounced** (pitched).
If it pitched **outside leg stump**: **NOT OUT** — no matter what else happens.
If it pitched **in line** with the stumps or **outside off stump**: LBW is still possible.
A **full toss** has not pitched, so this step does not stop it.
cards.fact: For a right-handed batter, leg stump is the stump nearest their legs.

cards.title: Step 3: Where did it hit the batter?
body: **In line** with the stumps: LBW is possible.
**Outside leg stump**: **NOT OUT**.
**Outside off stump**: out only if the batter made **no genuine attempt to play the ball** with the bat.
So if the batter **plays a shot** and is hit outside off stump, it is **not out**.

cards.title: Step 4: Would it hit the stumps?
body: The umpire imagines the path of the ball **if the batter's body was not there**.
If it would have gone on to **hit the stumps**, LBW can be given.
If it would have gone **over** the stumps or **past** them, it is **not out**.
Height and bounce matter — a ball hitting high on the thigh may go over the top.

cards.title: The umpire's view
body: The umpire at the **bowler's end** has the best view of the line of the ball.
If the umpire is **not sure**, the batter gets the **benefit of the doubt**: not out.
LBW decisions are some of the hardest in cricket, which is why technology like **ball-tracking** is used in top matches.

quiz.q: What does LBW stand for?
quiz.ex: LBW stands for Leg Before Wicket.

quiz.q: The ball pitches outside leg stump, then hits the pad in line and would hit the stumps. Out or not out?
quiz.ex: A ball pitching outside leg stump can never be out LBW.

quiz.q: The ball hits the bat first, then the pad, and would have hit the stumps. Is it LBW?
options: Only if the bowler appeals twice
quiz.ex: If the ball touches the bat first, the batter cannot be out LBW.

quiz.q: The ball pitches on off stump and hits the pad in line with the stumps. Ball-tracking shows it would hit middle stump. It was a legal ball. Decision?
quiz.ex: Pitched in line, hit in line, hitting the stumps, no bat first: all conditions are met — out.

quiz.q: The ball hits the pad outside off stump while the batter is playing a proper shot. It would have hit the stumps. Is it out?
options: Not out — impact outside off while playing a shot
quiz.ex: When impact is outside off stump, LBW is only out if the batter made no genuine attempt to play the ball.

quiz.q: The batter lifts the bat high and leaves the ball (no shot). It hits the pad outside off stump and would go on to hit the stumps. Decision?
options: Not out — impact outside off is never out
Not out — it is a wide
Out LBW — no shot was offered
quiz.ex: With no genuine attempt to play the ball, impact outside off stump can still be out LBW.

quiz.q: The ball hits the batter's pad, but it was bouncing so high it would have gone over the stumps. Decision?
quiz.ex: For LBW the ball must have been going on to hit the stumps. Going over the top is not out.

quiz.q: The umpire is not sure if the ball would have hit the stumps. What should they decide?
options: Out — the bowler gets the benefit
Not out — the batter gets the benefit of the doubt
quiz.ex: When in doubt, the decision goes in the batter's favour.

cards.title: Hit the ball twice
body: A batter is out **hit the ball twice** if they **deliberately** strike the ball a second time.
They are allowed to hit it again **only to protect their wicket** — for example stopping it rolling onto the stumps.
But they must not use a hand that is not holding the bat to do it.

cards.title: Obstructing the field
body: A batter is out **obstructing the field** if they **wilfully** block or distract a fielder by word or action.
Example: deliberately changing direction while running to block a throw.
Since 2017, **handled the ball** is part of this: wilfully hitting the ball with a hand not holding the bat (unless it is to avoid injury) is obstructing the field.
Picking up the ball to give it back to a fielder **without their permission** is obstructing the field too.

cards.title: Timed out
body: When a batter is out, the next batter must be **ready to face** quickly.
The Laws say within **3 minutes**. In men's international cricket, ICC rules say **2 minutes**.
If not, the fielding side can appeal and the new batter is **timed out**.
cards.fact: Angelo Mathews (Sri Lanka) became the first batter timed out in men's international cricket, against Bangladesh at the 2023 World Cup.

cards.title: Retired hurt vs retired out
body: **Retired hurt**: a batter leaves because of **injury or illness**. They are **not out** and may come back later to continue.
**Retired out**: a batter leaves for **any other reason** (not injury or illness). Unless the other captain lets them return, they are **retired out** and it counts as a wicket.

cards.title: Running out the non-striker
body: The **non-striker** should stay in their ground until the bowler would normally **release the ball**.
If they leave early, the bowler can break the wicket at their end — that is **run out** under **Law 38**.
It used to be listed under 'unfair play', but since 2022 it is simply a normal **run out**.
Good habit: keep your bat in the crease until the ball leaves the bowler's hand.

cards.title: Fair play rules
body: **No saliva**: fielders may not use spit to shine the ball (sweat is still allowed).
**5 penalty runs** are given to the batting side if the ball hits a **fielder's helmet** lying on the ground.
**Fake fielding** — pretending to field or throw the ball to fool the batters — also gives the batters **5 penalty runs**.

cards.title: The Spirit of Cricket
body: Cricket has a special idea called the **Spirit of Cricket**.
It means **respect**: for your opponents, your teammates, the umpires and the game.
Accept the umpire's decision, play hard but fair, and **shake hands** at the end.
Captains are responsible for making sure their team plays in this spirit.
cards.fact: The Spirit of Cricket is written at the very start of the Laws of Cricket.

quiz.q: A batter blocks the ball, then deliberately hits it again towards the boundary to score runs. What happens?
quiz.ex: Deliberately hitting the ball a second time (not to protect the wicket) is out, hit the ball twice.

quiz.q: Since 2017, 'handled the ball' has been merged into which dismissal?
quiz.ex: Handled the ball is now part of obstructing the field.

quiz.q: Under the Laws of Cricket, how long does a new batter have to be ready to face?
quiz.ex: The Laws say 3 minutes. ICC men's international playing conditions use 2 minutes.

quiz.q: Who was the first batter timed out in men's international cricket?
quiz.ex: Angelo Mathews of Sri Lanka was timed out against Bangladesh at the 2023 World Cup.

quiz.q: A batter twists an ankle and leaves the field. Later, they come back to bat. What was this called?
quiz.ex: Retired hurt is for injury or illness. The batter is not out and can return.

quiz.q: The non-striker leaves the crease before the bowler releases the ball. The bowler breaks the wicket at that end. How is the non-striker out?
quiz.ex: Under Law 38 (2022 update), this is a run out.

quiz.q: The ball hits a fielder's helmet that is lying on the ground. What happens?
options: 5 penalty runs to the batting side
quiz.ex: The batting side is awarded 5 penalty runs.

quiz.q: Fielders are allowed to use saliva (spit) to shine the ball.
quiz.ex: False. Using saliva on the ball is not allowed.

cards.title: The match officials
body: Two **on-field umpires** run the game: one at the **bowler's end** and one at **square leg**.
The **third umpire** watches TV replays to help with run outs, stumpings, boundaries and reviews.
The **match referee** makes sure players follow the rules of conduct and can hand out penalties.
The umpires' decisions are final on the field.

cards.title: DRS: reviewing decisions
body: **DRS** means **Decision Review System**. It is used in many top international matches.
A **batter** or the **fielding captain** can ask for a review by making a **"T"** sign with their hands.
The third umpire uses replays, **ball-tracking** and edge detection to check the decision.
If the review shows the decision was wrong, it is changed.

cards.title: Umpire's call
body: Sometimes ball-tracking shows an LBW is **very close** — for example the ball only just clipping the stumps.
Then the **on-field decision stays** — this is called **umpire's call**.
On umpire's call, the reviewing team **keeps** its review — it does not count as a lost review.

cards.title: Signals: out and boundaries
body: **Out**: the umpire raises an **index finger** above the head.
**Four**: the umpire **waves one arm** from side to side across the chest.
**Six**: the umpire raises **both arms** straight above the head.

cards.title: Signals: extras
body: **Wide**: **both arms** stretched out sideways.
**No-ball**: **one arm** stretched out sideways.
**Bye**: an **open hand** raised above the head.
**Leg-bye**: the umpire **touches a raised knee** with the hand.

cards.title: Signals: more to know
body: **Dead ball**: **crossing and uncrossing the wrists** below the waist.
**Short run**: bending one arm up and **touching the shoulder** with the fingertips.
**Free hit**: raising one arm and moving it in a **circle**.
**Penalty runs**: **tapping a shoulder** with the opposite hand.
cards.fact: Scorers watch the umpire's signals and wave back to show they have understood.

quiz.q: The umpire raises both arms straight above the head. What does it mean?
quiz.ex: Both arms raised above the head is the signal for six.

quiz.q: The umpire stretches ONE arm out sideways. What has been called?
quiz.ex: One arm out sideways is a no-ball. Both arms out is a wide.

quiz.q: The umpire touches a raised knee with their hand. What is the signal?
quiz.ex: Touching a raised knee is the leg-bye signal.

quiz.q: What does the umpire do to give a batter out?
options: Wave an arm across the chest
Raise an index finger above the head
quiz.ex: A raised index finger means out.

quiz.q: Who watches TV replays to help decide close run outs?
quiz.ex: The third umpire uses replays to check run outs, stumpings, boundaries and reviews.

quiz.q: How does a player ask for a DRS review?
options: By making a 'T' sign with their hands
quiz.ex: A 'T' sign with the hands asks for a review.

quiz.q: A team reviews an LBW. Ball-tracking shows the ball just clipping the stumps, so the result is 'umpire's call'. What happens to their review?
quiz.ex: On umpire's call the on-field decision stays, and the reviewing team keeps its review.

quiz.q: The umpire raises one arm and moves it in a circle. What does it mean?
quiz.ex: A circular motion with a raised arm signals a free hit.

cards.title: Test cricket
body: A **Test** is played over up to **5 days**.
Each team gets **two innings**, and there is no limit on overs per innings.
To win, you usually need to **bowl the other team out twice**.
If time runs out first, the match is a **draw**.

cards.title: The follow-on
body: If the team batting second is a **long way behind** after the first innings, the other captain can make them **bat again straight away**.
This is called **enforcing the follow-on**.
In a 5-day Test, the lead must be at least **200 runs**.
It saves time, giving the stronger team a better chance to win before the match ends.

cards.title: ODI fielding restrictions
body: In ODIs, fielding limits are set by **powerplays**, counting fielders **outside the 30-yard circle**:
**Overs 1–10**: at most **2** fielders outside the circle.
**Overs 11–40**: at most **4** fielders outside.
**Overs 41–50**: at most **5** fielders outside.

cards.title: T20 fielding restrictions
body: In T20Is, the **powerplay** is the **first 6 overs**: at most **2** fielders outside the circle.
After the powerplay: at most **5** fielders outside.
In every format, Law 28.4 says no more than **2 fielders behind square on the leg side** (not counting the keeper).
cards.fact: Powerplays are when batters attack hardest — the gaps in the outfield are open!

cards.title: The super over
body: If a limited-overs match is **tied** and a winner is needed, a **super over** may be played.
Each team bats for **one over** to decide the winner.
Not every tied match uses a super over — it depends on the competition's rules.

cards.title: Rain and DLS
body: If **rain** cuts overs from a limited-overs match, the target may be changed.
This uses the **DLS** method (**Duckworth–Lewis–Stern**).
DLS looks at a team's **resources**: the **overs** and **wickets** they have left.
The chasing team gets a **revised target** that is fair for the overs they can still face.
cards.fact: Losing overs is bad for a team, but having lots of wickets left is good — DLS counts both.

quiz.q: How many innings does each team get in a Test match?
quiz.ex: In a Test, each team can bat twice.

quiz.q: In a 5-day Test, how big a first-innings lead is needed to enforce the follow-on?
quiz.ex: In a 5-day match, the lead must be at least 200 runs.

quiz.q: In ODI overs 1–10, how many fielders may be outside the 30-yard circle?
quiz.ex: Overs 1–10 in an ODI allow a maximum of 2 fielders outside the circle.

quiz.q: In ODI overs 11–40, how many fielders may be outside the 30-yard circle?
quiz.ex: Overs 11–40 allow a maximum of 4 fielders outside the circle.

quiz.q: Look at the picture: 5 fielders are outside the circle. It is the 3rd over of a T20I. Is this field legal?
options: No — only 2 are allowed outside in the powerplay
quiz.ex: In the T20I powerplay (first 6 overs), at most 2 fielders may be outside the circle.

quiz.q: In a T20I, how many overs does the powerplay last?
quiz.ex: The T20I powerplay is the first 6 overs.

quiz.q: A limited-overs knockout match is tied and a winner is needed. What may decide it?
options: The team with more sixes always wins
quiz.ex: A super over, where each team bats for one over, may be played to decide the winner.

quiz.q: What does the DLS method look at to set a revised target after rain?
options: Only the number of sixes hit
The resources left: overs and wickets
quiz.ex: DLS uses a team's resources — overs and wickets remaining — to set a fair revised target.

modules.title: Field Positions
modules.desc: Learn every fielding position, from the slips to cow corner, and how captains set a field.

cards.title: Two halves of the field
body: Imagine a line running straight down the middle of the pitch, from wicket to wicket, and on past both ends.
It splits the field into two halves: the **off side** and the **leg side**.
The **off side** is the side the batter's chest faces when standing ready.
The **leg side** (also called the **on side**) is the side behind the batter's legs.
cards.fact: All the directions in this lesson are for a right-handed batter.

cards.title: Left-handers flip everything
body: A **left-handed** batter stands the other way round.
So for a left-hander the off side and the leg side **swap**, like a mirror.
When a left-hander comes in, the fielders change sides of the field.
So the off side for a right-hander is the leg side for a left-hander.
cards.fact: That is why you often see fielders jogging across the field when a right-hander and a left-hander are batting together and they take a single.

cards.title: Square, in front and behind
body: **Square** means level with the batter, along the line of the popping crease stretched out to the boundary.
**In front of square** means on the bowler's side of that line.
**Behind square** means on the wicket-keeper's side of that line.
**Point** stands square on the off side and **square leg** stands square on the leg side.

cards.title: Fine, square and straight
body: **Fine** means close to the line of the pitch, behind the batter, near the keeper's direction.
**Straight** means close to the line of the pitch in front, towards the bowler's end.
**Square** is in between: out to the side, level with the batter.
So **fine leg** is behind the batter on the leg side, and **long-on** is straight down the ground on the leg side.

cards.title: Close, ring and deep
body: **Silly** means very, very close to the batter, like **silly point**.
**Short** means close in, like **short leg**.
The **ring** is the group of fielders saving the single, about 30 yards from the batter.
**Deep** or **long** means out near the boundary, like **deep cover** or **long-off**.
cards.fact: Close fielders wear a helmet because the ball can come at them very fast.

cards.title: Infield and outfield
body: In limited-overs cricket a **30-yard circle** is marked on the ground.
The area inside the circle is the **infield**.
The area between the circle and the boundary is the **outfield**.
Rules about how many fielders may stand outside the circle are called **fielding restrictions**.

quiz.q: For a right-handed batter, the off side is...
options: The side behind the batter's legs
The side the batter's chest faces
Always the side nearest the pavilion
quiz.ex: The off side is the side the batter faces when standing ready. The leg side is behind the legs.

quiz.q: What is another name for the leg side?
quiz.ex: The leg side is also called the on side, which is why we have mid-on and long-on.

quiz.q: A left-handed batter comes in to bat. What happens to the off side and leg side?
options: There is no off side for left-handers
quiz.ex: A left-hander stands the other way round, so the off and leg sides swap and fielders change positions.

quiz.q: Both marked fielders are on the wicket-keeper's side of the popping-crease line. Where are they?
quiz.ex: Behind square means on the keeper's side of the line through the popping crease.

quiz.q: This fielder is very, very close to the batter on the off side. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Silly means very close, so this is silly point. Deep and long mean near the boundary.

quiz.q: This fielder stands square on the off side. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Point stands level with the batter on the off side.

quiz.q: This fielder is behind square, close to the line of the pitch, on the leg side, near the boundary. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Fine means close to the line of the pitch behind the batter. Fine leg is on the leg side near the boundary.

quiz.q: True or false: the outfield is the area inside the 30-yard circle.
quiz.ex: Inside the circle is the infield. The outfield is between the circle and the boundary.

cards.title: The wicket-keeper
body: The **wicket-keeper** stands behind the batter's stumps and catches every ball the batter misses.
The keeper is the only fielder allowed to wear **gloves** and **external leg guards**.
The keeper catches edges, stumps batters and takes throws at the stumps.
The keeper must not take the ball in front of the stumps before it has passed the wicket or touched the bat or batter.
cards.fact: If the keeper takes the ball in front of the stumps too early, it is a no-ball.

cards.title: The slips
body: The **slips** stand in a line next to the keeper, on the off side.
**First slip** is closest to the keeper, then **second slip**, then **third slip**.
They are there to catch the **outside edge**, when the ball just nicks the bat and flies backwards.
Fast bowlers love slips because the ball comes off the edge quickly.

cards.title: Gully and fly slip
body: **Gully** stands a little wider and squarer than the slips, on the off side.
Gully catches thick edges and hard cuts that fly off the bat.
**Fly slip** stands much deeper than the slips, between the slips and third man.
Fly slip catches edges that fly high and far over the slips.

cards.title: Leg slip and leg gully
body: **Leg slip** is like a first slip, but on the **leg side**, next to the keeper.
**Leg gully** is a little squarer than leg slip on the leg side.
They catch glances and edges that go fine on the leg side.
Spinners and bowlers attacking the batter's legs often use them.

cards.title: Short leg and silly point
body: **Short leg** stands very close on the leg side, next to the batter's hip.
**Silly point** stands very close on the off side, opposite short leg.
They wait for **bat-pad catches**: the ball hits the bat and pad and pops up gently.
These fielders wear a **helmet** and protective gear because they are so close.
cards.fact: Short leg is often called the bravest position on the field!

cards.title: Silly mid-off and silly mid-on
body: **Silly mid-off** stands very close in front of the batter on the off side.
**Silly mid-on** stands very close in front of the batter on the leg side.
They catch the ball when a batter pushes forward and the ball pops up off the bat.
Spinners use them to put **pressure** on a nervous batter.

quiz.q: Which is the only fielder allowed to wear gloves and external leg guards?
quiz.ex: Only the wicket-keeper may wear gloves and external leg guards.

quiz.q: Why do slips stand next to the keeper?
quiz.ex: Slips catch the ball when it nicks the outside edge of the bat and flies backwards.

quiz.q: This fielder stands closest to the keeper in the slips. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: First slip is the slip fielder right next to the keeper.

quiz.q: A ball hits the batter's bat and pad and pops up gently near the batter's hip on the leg side. Which fielder is waiting for this catch?
quiz.ex: Short leg stands very close on the leg side for bat-pad catches.

quiz.q: Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Silly point stands very close to the batter, square on the off side.

quiz.q: This fielder stands deeper than the slips, to catch high edges. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Fly slip stands much deeper than the slips, between the slips and third man.

quiz.q: This close fielder is like first slip, but on the other side. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Leg slip is the leg-side version of first slip, standing next to the keeper.

quiz.q: The keeper takes the ball in front of the stumps before it reaches the wicket or touches the bat. What is it?
quiz.ex: The keeper must wait until the ball has passed the wicket or touched the bat or batter. Otherwise it is a no-ball.

cards.title: What is the ring?
body: The **ring** is the group of fielders standing around the **30-yard circle**.
Their main job is **saving the single**: stopping the batters taking easy runs.
They walk in a few steps as the bowler runs up, so they are moving and ready.
A quick pick-up and throw can turn a single into a **run out**.

cards.title: Point and backward point
body: **Point** stands square on the off side, level with the batter.
**Backward point** stands a little **behind square** on the off side.
Both stop square cuts and catch balls that fly off the bat.
Point is one of the busiest spots for quick, sharp fielders.

cards.title: Cover and extra cover
body: **Cover** stands in front of square on the off side, between point and mid-off.
**Extra cover** stands between cover and mid-off.
These fielders stop **cover drives**, one of the most popular shots.
Teams often put their best fielder at cover.

cards.title: Mid-off and mid-on
body: **Mid-off** stands in front of the batter on the off side, near the bowler.
**Mid-on** stands in the same kind of place on the leg side.
They stop straight drives and catch mistimed lofted shots.
The captain often fields at mid-off or mid-on to talk to the bowler.

cards.title: Mid-wicket and square leg
body: **Mid-wicket** stands on the leg side between mid-on and square leg.
**Square leg** stands square on the leg side, level with the batter.
They stop flicks and pulls through the leg side.
The square-leg umpire stands near square leg too, so the fielder keeps out of the umpire's way.

cards.title: Short fine leg
body: **Short fine leg** stands inside the circle, behind square on the leg side.
It stops glances and edges going fine on the leg side.
It saves the single, while **fine leg** (out on the boundary) saves the four.
Batters love to glance the ball off their pads here for an easy single.

quiz.q: What is the main job of the fielders in the ring?
options: Catching edges next to the keeper
quiz.ex: Ring fielders stand around the 30-yard circle to stop the batters taking easy singles.

quiz.q: Why do ring fielders walk in a few steps as the bowler runs up?
options: So they are moving and ready to react
quiz.ex: Walking in means they are already moving and can react faster to the ball.

quiz.q: Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Cover is in front of square on the off side, between point and mid-off.

quiz.q: This fielder is on the leg side, between mid-on and square leg. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Mid-wicket stands on the leg side between mid-on and square leg.

quiz.q: Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Backward point is just behind square on the off side, inside the ring.

quiz.q: This fielder is inside the circle, behind square on the leg side. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Short fine leg is inside the circle. Fine leg is the deep version out on the boundary.

quiz.q: This fielder stands near the bowler on the off side. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Mid-off is in front of the batter on the off side, near the bowler. Mid-on is on the leg side.

quiz.q: Which fielder stands square on the leg side, level with the batter?
quiz.ex: Square leg stands square on the leg side. Point is its partner on the off side.

cards.title: Guarding the boundary
body: **Deep** fielders stand near the boundary rope.
Their job is **saving the boundary**: stopping fours and catching big hits.
A deep fielder who stops a four and lets the batters run one has saved three runs!
They need a strong, accurate throw back to the keeper or bowler.

cards.title: Third man and deep point
body: **Third man** stands deep behind square on the off side, fine of the slips area.
Third man stops edges that run past the slips and late cuts.
**Deep point** stands square on the off side, out on the boundary.
Deep point stops hard square cuts.

cards.title: Deep cover, long-off and long-on
body: **Deep cover** guards the cover boundary against big drives.
**Long-off** stands straight on the off side, near the sight screen.
**Long-on** stands straight on the leg side, near the sight screen.
Long-off and long-on catch big lofted drives hit back over the bowler's head.

cards.title: Cow corner and deep mid-wicket
body: **Cow corner** is on the leg side, between long-on and deep mid-wicket.
Batters swinging hard **across the line** often hit the ball there, so it is a busy spot in big-hitting overs.
**Deep mid-wicket** guards the leg side against pulls and big slog shots.
These are great places for catches when batters try to hit sixes.

cards.title: Deep square leg and fine leg
body: **Deep square leg** stands square on the leg side, near the boundary.
It stops pulls and sweeps and catches top-edged hooks.
**Fine leg** stands deep behind square on the leg side.
Fine leg stops glances, sweeps and hooks that go fine.

cards.title: Catching on the boundary
body: Watch the ball all the way into your hands. Keep your **fingers pointing up** for a high catch near your face.
If you touch the ball while you are touching the **boundary rope**, it counts as a boundary.
So a boundary fielder must know where the rope is before the ball arrives.
If the ball reaches the boundary after bouncing it is **4**. If it crosses on the full it is **6**.
cards.fact: Many great boundary catches are taken by fielders who stay calm and watch the ball, not the rope.

quiz.q: What is the main job of the deep fielders?
options: Saving the boundary and catching big hits
quiz.ex: Deep fielders stand near the rope to stop fours and catch big hits.

quiz.q: This fielder stands deep behind square on the off side. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Third man is deep and behind square on the off side, stopping edges past the slips.

quiz.q: This fielder stands straight down the ground on the leg side, near the boundary. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Long-on is straight and deep on the leg side. Long-off is its partner on the off side.

quiz.q: Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Cow corner is on the leg side, between long-on and deep mid-wicket.

quiz.q: This fielder stands square on the off side, out on the boundary. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Deep point is square on the off side near the rope. Point is the ring version.

quiz.q: A fielder catches the ball but is touching the boundary rope at the same time. What is it?
quiz.ex: Touching the ball while touching the boundary counts as a boundary, not a catch.

quiz.q: A deep fielder stops a ball that was going for four, and the batters run one. How many runs did the fielder save?
quiz.ex: It would have been 4. Only 1 was scored, so the fielder saved 3 runs.

quiz.q: This fielder stands deep behind square on the leg side. Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Fine leg is deep on the leg side behind square. Short fine leg is the one inside the circle.

cards.title: Attack or defend?
body: The captain and bowler decide where the **11 fielders** stand. That includes the bowler and the keeper.
An **attacking field** has lots of catchers close to the bat to take wickets.
A **defensive field** has more fielders in the deep to stop runs.
Captains attack when a new batter comes in and defend when batters are scoring fast.

cards.title: Fast bowler with slips
body: A fast bowler with a new ball often has **two or three slips** and a **gully**.
The ball swings and bounces, so edges are likely.
Other fielders might be at **point**, **cover**, **mid-off**, **mid-on** and **fine leg**.
As the ball gets older, the captain may take slips away and push fielders back.

cards.title: Spinner with close fielders
body: A spinner often has fielders right next to the bat: **short leg**, **silly point** and a **slip**.
Spin makes the ball pop up off the bat and pad.
The keeper stands right up to the stumps, ready for a **stumping**.
This puts lots of pressure on the batter.

cards.title: Death-over fields
body: The **death overs** are the last few overs of a limited-overs innings, when batters hit out.
Captains put fielders out on the boundary, such as **long-on**, **long-off**, **deep mid-wicket**, **deep square leg** and **deep point**.
Bowlers try **yorkers** and slower balls to stop the big hits.
The fielding restrictions still limit how many can be out on the boundary.
cards.fact: Jasprit Bumrah is famous for his deadly yorkers at the death.

cards.title: Powerplay limits
body: In **ODIs**: overs **1–10**, at most **2** fielders outside the 30-yard circle.
ODI overs **11–40**: at most **4** outside. Overs **41–50**: at most **5** outside.
In **T20Is**: the first **6 overs** are the powerplay, with at most **2** outside the circle.
After the T20I powerplay, at most **5** fielders may be outside the circle.
cards.fact: These limits make it easier for batters to score at the start of an innings.

cards.title: Law 28.4: behind square on the leg side
body: At the moment the ball is bowled, no more than **2 fielders** (not counting the keeper) may be **behind square on the leg side**.
Behind square here means behind the popping crease.
If the fielding side breaks this Law, the umpire calls **no-ball**.
Positions behind square on the leg side include **fine leg**, **short fine leg**, **leg slip**, **leg gully** and **deep square leg** when it is behind square.

cards.title: Stay still once the bowler starts
body: Once the bowler starts the **run-up**, fielders must not make big moves to a new position.
Small steps and **walking in** towards the batter are fine.
A fielder may move early when they can see which shot the batter is about to play.
If a fielder moves unfairly, the umpire calls **dead ball** and the batting side gets **5 penalty runs**.

quiz.q: An attacking field has...
options: Lots of fielders on the boundary
Lots of catchers close to the bat
No fielders on the off side
quiz.ex: Attacking fields put catchers near the bat to take wickets. Defensive fields have more fielders deep.

quiz.q: A fast bowler has a brand new ball. Which positions are marked?
quiz.ex: Fast bowlers with a new ball often use slips and gully to catch edges.

quiz.q: A spinner is bowling. Which close fielders are marked?
quiz.ex: Spinners use short leg and silly point for bat-pad catches.

quiz.q: In an ODI, how many fielders may be outside the 30-yard circle in overs 1–10?
options: As many as the captain wants
quiz.ex: In ODI overs 1–10, at most 2 fielders may be outside the circle.

quiz.q: In a T20I after the first 6 overs, what is the most fielders allowed outside the circle?
quiz.ex: After the 6-over powerplay in a T20I, up to 5 fielders may be outside the circle.

quiz.q: At the moment of delivery the captain has 3 fielders behind square on the leg side (not counting the keeper). What does the umpire call?
quiz.ex: Law 28.4 allows at most 2 fielders behind square on the leg side. Breaking it is a no-ball.

quiz.q: It's the death overs. Where would a captain mostly put the fielders shown?
quiz.ex: In the death overs batters hit out, so captains push fielders back to the boundary.

quiz.q: True or false: after the bowler starts the run-up, fielders may walk in a few steps towards the batter.
quiz.ex: Small steps and walking in are fine. Big moves to a new position are not allowed.

modules.title: Batting
modules.desc: Grip, stance, every classic and modern shot, and smart running between the wickets.

cards.title: The V grip
body: Hold the bat with **both hands close together** near the top of the handle.
Your thumb and first finger make a **V shape** on each hand.
The two Vs should **line up** down the back of the handle.
For a right-hander, the left hand is on top and the right hand is below it.
cards.fact: A good grip helps the bat come down straight.

cards.title: Top hand in charge
body: The **top hand** controls the bat. It guides the bat straight.
The **bottom hand** holds more lightly. It adds power, but too much can twist the bat.
A tight bottom hand often makes the ball go in the air.
Think: top hand steers, bottom hand helps.

cards.title: The stance
body: Stand **side-on**, with your front shoulder pointing at the bowler.
Feet about **shoulder-width apart**, one each side of the crease.
Knees slightly **bent**, weight balanced on the balls of your feet.
Rest the bat near your back toe, ready to lift.

cards.title: Taking guard
body: Before facing, you ask the umpire for your **guard**. This tells you where you are standing compared with the stumps.
**Leg stump** guard (one leg): bat lined up with leg stump.
**Middle and leg** guard (two legs): bat between middle and leg stumps.
**Middle** guard (centre): bat lined up with middle stump.
Batters scratch a mark on the crease so they can find their guard every ball.

cards.title: The backlift
body: As the bowler runs in, you lift the bat back. This is the **backlift**.
Lift it **straight back** towards the stumps or slips, not out towards square leg.
A good backlift lets the bat come down straight and in time.
Keep your hands relaxed, not stiff.

cards.title: Head still, watch the ball
body: Keep your **head still** and your **eyes level**.
**Watch the ball** right from the bowler's hand onto the bat.
A moving head makes it much harder to judge the ball.
Great batters say: watch the ball, then play the shot.
cards.fact: Watching the ball out of the bowler's hand helps you spot swing and spin early.

quiz.q: In the V grip, the two Vs made by your thumbs and first fingers should...
options: Be at opposite ends of the handle
Line up down the back of the handle
quiz.ex: Both Vs should line up, with the hands close together near the top of the handle.

quiz.q: For a right-handed batter, which hand goes on top?
quiz.ex: A right-hander has the left hand on top and the right hand below it.

quiz.q: Which hand controls and steers the bat?
quiz.ex: The top hand is in charge. The bottom hand helps with power.

quiz.q: A batter keeps hitting the ball in the air because they grip too hard with one hand. Which hand is probably too tight?
quiz.ex: A tight bottom hand can twist the bat and lift the ball into the air.

quiz.q: How should a batter stand in the stance?
options: Side-on, front shoulder pointing at the bowler
quiz.ex: A good stance is side-on, with the front shoulder pointing at the bowler.

quiz.q: A batter asks the umpire for 'two legs'. Which guard is that?
quiz.ex: Two legs means middle and leg guard: the bat between middle and leg stumps.

quiz.q: Where should the backlift go?
options: Straight back towards the stumps or slips
quiz.ex: A straight backlift helps the bat come down straight.

quiz.q: True or false: keeping your head still makes it easier to judge the ball.
quiz.ex: A still head with level eyes lets you watch the ball clearly from the bowler's hand.

cards.title: When to go forward
body: Play on the **front foot** when the ball is **pitched up**: a **full** ball or a **half-volley**.
A **half-volley** bounces just in front of you, so you can hit it right after it bounces.
Step your front foot towards where the ball pitches.
Lead with your **head** over the front knee.

cards.title: Forward defence
body: The **forward defence** stops a good ball from getting you out.
Step forward to the pitch of the ball, front knee bent.
Bat comes down straight, **close to the front pad**, angled down.
Use **soft hands** so the ball drops near your feet.
cards.fact: Defence is not boring. It keeps you in, and runs come later!

cards.title: Straight drive
body: The **straight drive** is played to a full ball on the line of the stumps.
Step forward and swing the bat straight through the line.
The ball goes back past the bowler, straight down the ground.
Finish with the bat high and your head still.

cards.title: Cover drive and off drive
body: The **cover drive** is played to a full ball **outside off stump**.
Step towards the ball and swing through, sending it through **extra cover** or cover.
The **off drive** is played to a full ball just outside off, hit between the bowler and **mid-off**.
Keep the ball on the ground by having your head over the ball.

cards.title: On drive
body: The **on drive** is played to a full ball on **middle or leg stump**.
The ball goes towards **mid-on**, on the leg side.
It's one of the hardest drives. Keep your front shoulder pointing at the ball.
Lead with the top hand and keep the bat straight.

cards.title: Lofted drive
body: The **lofted drive** hits the ball over the fielders, often over **long-on** or **long-off**.
Get right to the pitch of the ball and swing through with a full follow-through.
The ball goes in the air, so there is a risk of being caught.
Only go aerial when there are no fielders in the deep in that area, or when you are sure of the six.

cards.title: The sweep
body: The **sweep** is played mostly against spin, to a full ball around **leg stump**.
Go down on your **back knee**, front leg stretched forward.
Swing the bat across and sweep the ball round towards **square leg** or **fine leg**.
Watch out: if you miss and the ball hits your pad, you can be out LBW.

quiz.q: Which kind of ball should you usually play on the front foot?
quiz.ex: Front-foot shots are played to pitched-up balls: full balls and half-volleys.

quiz.q: In the forward defence, where should the bat be?
options: Close to the front pad, angled down
quiz.ex: The bat comes down close to the front pad, angled down, with soft hands.

quiz.q: Which shot sends the ball this way?
quiz.ex: The cover drive sends a full ball outside off stump through extra cover.

quiz.q: Which shot sends the ball this way?
quiz.ex: The straight drive sends the ball straight back past the bowler.

quiz.q: A full ball is bowled on middle and leg stump. Which drive should you play?
quiz.ex: The on drive is played to a full ball on middle or leg stump, towards mid-on.

quiz.q: Which shot sends the ball this way?
quiz.ex: The sweep goes down on one knee and sends the ball round towards square leg.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of a lofted drive?
quiz.ex: A lofted drive goes in the air, so a fielder could catch it.

quiz.q: A batter sweeps, misses, and the ball hits the pad in line with the stumps. What could happen?
options: It is automatically four leg byes
The batter could be out LBW
quiz.ex: Missing the sweep and getting hit on the pad can lead to an LBW dismissal.

cards.title: When to go back
body: Play on the **back foot** when the ball is **short**: it bounces further from you and comes up higher.
Step your back foot **back and across** towards off stump.
This gives you more time to see the ball.
Stay balanced and keep your head still.

cards.title: Backward defence
body: The **backward defence** blocks a short ball that is on the stumps.
Step back and across, standing tall.
Keep a **high front elbow** and the bat straight.
Use soft hands so the ball drops down in front of you.

cards.title: Square cut and late cut
body: The **square cut** is played to a short, **wide** ball outside off stump.
Step back and across, then slash the bat down hard on the ball, sending it towards **point**.
The **late cut** waits until the ball is almost past you, then guides it fine towards **third man**.
Cuts need the ball to be wide. Cutting a ball close to the stumps is risky.

cards.title: Pull and hook
body: The **pull** is played to a short ball around **waist height**, hit across to **mid-wicket** or square leg.
The **hook** is played to a short ball at **shoulder or head height**, usually towards **fine leg** or square leg.
The hook is risky: the ball often goes in the air to the deep fielders.
**Safety first**: always wear a **helmet**. If the short ball is too fast or too high, **duck or sway** out of the way.
cards.fact: Never take your eyes off a short ball. Watching it keeps you safe.

cards.title: Back-foot punch
body: The **back-foot punch** is played to a ball that is a little short, outside off stump.
Go back, stand tall, and punch the ball with a short, firm swing.
The ball goes through the **cover** area, along the ground.
It's a great shot on bouncy pitches.

cards.title: Leg glance and flick
body: The **leg glance** gently guides a ball on your legs **fine**, past the keeper, towards **fine leg**.
Just turn the bat face as the ball arrives. Let the ball's speed do the work.
The glance can be played off the front or back foot.
The **flick** uses the wrists to whip a ball on your pads towards **mid-wicket**.

quiz.q: Which kind of ball should you usually play on the back foot?
quiz.ex: Back-foot shots are played to short balls, which give you more time.

quiz.q: Which shot sends the ball this way?
quiz.ex: The square cut slashes a short, wide ball out towards point.

quiz.q: Which shot sends the ball this way?
quiz.ex: The pull hits a short ball at waist height across to mid-wicket.

quiz.q: Which shot sends the ball this way?
quiz.ex: The late cut waits until the ball is almost past and guides it fine to third man.

quiz.q: Which shot sends the ball this way?
quiz.ex: The leg glance turns the bat face to guide the ball fine on the leg side.

quiz.q: A short ball is coming at your head and it's too fast to play. What should you do?
options: Duck or sway out of the way, watching the ball
quiz.ex: If a short ball is too fast or high, duck or sway, but keep watching it. Always wear a helmet.

quiz.q: What is the difference between the pull and the hook?
options: The pull is for waist-height balls; the hook is for shoulder or head-height balls
The pull is a front-foot shot
quiz.ex: Both are played to short balls, but the hook is for higher ones, around shoulder or head height.

quiz.q: In the backward defence, what should the front elbow be?
quiz.ex: A high front elbow keeps the bat straight in the backward defence.

cards.title: Why new shots?
body: In T20 and ODI cricket, batters need to score fast, so they invented **new shots**.
These shots hit the ball to places where there are no fielders.
They have big **reward** (lots of runs) but also big **risk** (getting out).
Learn the proper shots first. Clever shots work best for batters with great basics.

cards.title: Reverse sweep and switch hit
body: In the **reverse sweep**, the batter turns the bat around and sweeps the ball to the **off side**, towards **backward point** or third man.
In the **switch hit**, the batter changes stance and grip to become a **left-hander** (or right-hander) as the bowler bowls.
Both surprise the fielding captain, who set the field for the normal side.
They are hard to do and you can easily miss the ball.

cards.title: Scoop, ramp and the Dilscoop
body: The **scoop** or **ramp** lifts the ball over the keeper or the slips, using the bowler's pace.
Sri Lanka's **Tillakaratne Dilshan** became famous for scooping the ball straight over the keeper's head: the **Dilscoop**.
The ball usually goes to **fine leg** or **third man**, where fielders are often missing.
It's very risky: if you get it wrong the ball can hit you, so a helmet is a must.

cards.title: The helicopter shot
body: **MS Dhoni** of India made the **helicopter shot** famous.
He flicks a full ball, often a yorker, with a very fast whip of the **wrists**.
The bat twirls round over his head at the end, like a helicopter's blades!
The ball usually flies over the leg side, towards **long-on** or mid-wicket.

cards.title: Slog sweep and upper cut
body: The **slog sweep** is a big sweep hit high over the leg side, towards **cow corner** or deep mid-wicket.
It is mostly played against spinners.
The **upper cut** is played to a short ball outside off stump: the batter lifts it over the slips towards **third man**.
Both can bring sixes but are often caught in the deep.

cards.title: Mr 360°
body: South Africa's **AB de Villiers** was called **Mr 360°**.
He could hit the ball **all the way round** the field, in every direction.
That made it almost impossible for captains to set a field for him.
His secret: brilliant basics, great balance and lots of practice.

cards.title: Risk vs reward
body: Every shot has a **risk** (chance of getting out) and a **reward** (runs).
A forward defence has low risk and low reward. A switch hit has high risk and high reward.
Smart batters choose risky shots only when the team needs fast runs.
Look at the field: hit the ball where the fielders **aren't**.

quiz.q: Who made the helicopter shot famous?
quiz.ex: India's MS Dhoni made the helicopter shot famous with his fast wrist-whip and twirling follow-through.

quiz.q: The Dilscoop is named after which batter?
quiz.ex: Sri Lanka's Tillakaratne Dilshan scooped the ball over the keeper's head: the Dilscoop.

quiz.q: Which shot sends the ball this way?
quiz.ex: The reverse sweep turns the bat around and sweeps the ball to the off side, towards backward point.

quiz.q: Which shot sends the ball this way?
quiz.ex: The slog sweep is a big sweep hit high over the leg side towards cow corner.

quiz.q: A batter changes from right-handed to left-handed stance and grip as the bowler bowls. What is this shot called?
quiz.ex: The switch hit means changing stance and grip to bat the other way round as the ball is bowled.

quiz.q: Which batter was called 'Mr 360°'?
quiz.ex: AB de Villiers could hit the ball all the way round the field, so he was called Mr 360°.

quiz.q: A short ball outside off stump is lifted over the slips towards third man. Which shot is it?
quiz.ex: The upper cut lifts a short ball outside off stump over the slips towards third man.

quiz.q: When should a smart batter try a high-risk shot?
options: When the team needs fast runs
Only in the first over of a Test
quiz.ex: Risky shots bring big rewards but can get you out, so use them when the team needs quick runs.

cards.title: Calling: Yes, No, Wait
body: Batters must talk to each other before running. This is **calling**.
**Yes!** means run. **No!** means stay. **Wait!** means hold on while you see where the ball goes.
After 'Wait', always follow with a clear **Yes** or **No**.
Call loudly and early, so your partner hears you.
cards.fact: Most run outs happen because batters did not call clearly.

cards.title: Who calls?
body: The batter with the **best view** of the ball makes the call.
If the ball goes **in front of square**, the **striker** calls.
If the ball goes **behind square**, the **non-striker** calls, because the striker can't see it well.
Trust your partner's call and run!

cards.title: Backing up
body: The **non-striker** walks a few steps forward as the bowler bowls. This is **backing up**.
It gives a head start for a quick single.
But stay in your crease until the ball has been released!
If the non-striker leaves the crease too early, the bowler can **run them out** (Law 38).

cards.title: Run hard, slide the bat
body: **Run the first run hard**: you might get a second or third run.
When you turn, **ground your bat** over the crease. If you don't, it's a **short run** and that run doesn't count.
Near the end of a run, **slide your bat** along the ground over the line. The bat reaches the crease before your feet.
Keep holding the bat when you slide: you're only safe if you're holding it or touching the ground behind the line.

cards.title: Rotating the strike
body: **Rotating the strike** means taking singles so both batters keep facing balls.
It stops bowlers settling into a rhythm against one batter.
Push the ball into gaps and run straight away.
Good batters make lots of runs this way, even without big hits.

cards.title: Batting average
body: **Batting average** = runs scored ÷ number of times **out**.
Innings where you are **not out** add runs but don't count as a time out.
Example: 150 runs in 6 innings, out 5 times (1 not out). Average = 150 ÷ 5 = **30**.
A higher average means a batter makes lots of runs before getting out.

cards.title: Strike rate
body: **Strike rate** = runs ÷ balls faced × 100.
It shows how **fast** a batter scores: runs per 100 balls.
In T20 cricket, a high strike rate is very important.

quiz.q: What are the three calls batters use when running?
quiz.ex: The calls are Yes (run), No (stay) and Wait (hold on, then Yes or No).

quiz.q: The striker plays a late cut towards third man, behind square. Who should call?
quiz.ex: For shots behind square the non-striker has the best view, so they call.

quiz.q: The striker drives the ball towards mid-off, in front of square. Who should call?
quiz.ex: For shots in front of square, the striker can see the ball best and calls.

quiz.q: The non-striker leaves the crease before the bowler releases the ball, and the bowler breaks the wicket. What happens?
options: The non-striker can be run out
quiz.ex: Under Law 38, leaving the crease too early means the non-striker can be run out.

quiz.q: A batter turns for a second run but forgets to ground the bat over the crease. What is it called?
quiz.ex: Not grounding the bat over the crease when turning is a short run, and that run doesn't count.

quiz.q: A batter has scored 200 runs in 5 innings and been out 4 times. What is the batting average?
quiz.ex: Average = runs ÷ times out = 200 ÷ 4 = 50. The not-out innings doesn't count as a time out.

quiz.q: A batter scores 30 runs off 20 balls. What is the strike rate?
quiz.ex: Strike rate = 30 ÷ 20 × 100 = 150.

quiz.q: What does 'rotating the strike' mean?
options: Taking singles so both batters keep facing
quiz.ex: Rotating the strike means taking singles so both batters keep facing and the bowler can't settle.

modules.title: Bowling
modules.desc: Bowl legally, hit your line and length, and master pace and spin.

cards.title: The five parts of a delivery
body: Every ball has five parts: the **run-up**, the **gather**, the **delivery stride**, the **release** and the **follow-through**.
The **run-up** builds rhythm and speed. Fast bowlers run in further than spinners.
The **gather** is the jump or bound where you load up your body, ready to bowl.
In the **delivery stride** your front foot lands and your arm comes over to **release** the ball.
The **follow-through** lets your body carry on smoothly after release, which helps protect your back.
cards.fact: Spinners often take just a few steps, but fast bowlers can run in a long way to build up pace.

cards.title: Bowl, don't throw!
body: In cricket the ball must be **bowled**, not thrown.
Your arm can bend a little naturally, but you must not straighten your elbow as you bowl.
The ICC allows a tiny amount of straightening: **no more than 15 degrees** of elbow extension.
If the umpire decides the ball was thrown, it is a **no-ball**.
cards.fact: 15 degrees is so small you usually can't see it. Experts test suspect actions with special cameras.

cards.title: Over or around the wicket
body: **Over the wicket**: your bowling arm is the one **nearest** the stumps at your end.
**Around the wicket**: your bowling arm is **farther** from the stumps.
You must tell the umpire which way and which arm you will bowl with, and the umpire tells the batter.
If you change without telling the umpire, it is a **no-ball**.

cards.title: Your feet and the no-ball
body: Front foot: some part of it must land **behind the popping crease** (it can be in the air over the line, but not all of it past the line).
Back foot: it must land **inside the return crease** and must not touch it.
Break either rule and the umpire calls **no-ball**: the batting side gets an extra run and, in ODIs and T20Is, the next ball is a **free hit**.
cards.fact: A no-ball also has to be bowled again, so it costs the bowler an extra ball too.

cards.title: Keep off the danger area
body: The middle part of the pitch is the **protected area**.
After you bowl, you must **not run on it** in your follow-through. Your spikes can damage the pitch and help your own spinners unfairly.
The umpire gives warnings. If a bowler keeps doing it, the bowler can be **taken off and banned from bowling** for the rest of the innings.
So in your follow-through, peel away to the side of the pitch.

cards.title: Not two overs in a row
body: An over is **6 legal balls**. Wides and no-balls don't count as one of the six.
After each over the ends change, and a **different bowler** must bowl the next over.
A bowler **cannot bowl two consecutive overs** in the same innings.
In limited-overs cricket there is also a maximum number of overs each bowler may bowl (for example 10 in an ODI and 4 in a T20).
cards.fact: A bowler can bowl one over, rest for one, then bowl again from the other end. That is how captains switch their bowlers around.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of a bowling action?
options: Gather, run-up, release, delivery stride, follow-through
Run-up, gather, delivery stride, release, follow-through
Run-up, release, gather, follow-through, delivery stride
quiz.ex: You run in, gather (load up), land in your delivery stride, release the ball, then follow through.

quiz.q: The ICC allows a bowler's elbow to straighten by up to how much?
quiz.ex: Elbow extension of more than 15 degrees means the ball is thrown, which is illegal.

quiz.q: A right-arm bowler runs in with their bowling arm right next to the stumps. How are they bowling?
quiz.ex: Over the wicket means the bowling arm is nearest the stumps.

quiz.q: A bowler suddenly switches from over to around the wicket without telling the umpire. What happens?
quiz.ex: The bowler must tell the umpire about any change of arm or side. Changing without telling is a no-ball.

quiz.q: The bowler's front foot lands with the heel just behind the popping crease and the toes over it. Is it a no-ball?
quiz.ex: Only some part of the front foot needs to be behind the popping crease, so a heel behind the line is fair.

quiz.q: What must a bowler NOT do in their follow-through?
options: Run on the protected area in the middle of the pitch
quiz.ex: Running on the protected area damages the pitch. Repeated offences can get a bowler banned from bowling for the rest of the innings.

quiz.q: True or false: a bowler may bowl two overs in a row if the captain says so.
quiz.ex: False. A bowler can never bowl two consecutive overs in the same innings.

quiz.q: A bowler bowls 6 balls, but one of them was a wide. How many more balls must they bowl to finish the over?
quiz.ex: Wides and no-balls are not part of the 6 legal balls, so one more ball is needed.

cards.title: What are line and length?
body: **Length** is how far down the pitch the ball bounces.
