**Line** is where the ball is heading from side to side: off stump, middle stump, leg stump, or wider.
Good bowlers control both. Most wickets come from accurate line and length, not just speed.
cards.fact: Bowlers practise by putting a target on the pitch and trying to hit it again and again.

cards.title: The lengths, from short to full
body: **Bouncer**: very short, so it rises towards the batter's shoulder or head.
**Short**: bounces well short and comes up high, easy to pull or cut if it's loose.
**Back of a length**: just short of a good length, hits the bat high and is hard to drive.
**Good length**: the batter can't decide whether to come forward or go back. This is the hardest length to face.
**Full**: pitches closer to the batter, good for swing but it can be driven.

cards.title: Right up at the toes
body: **Half-volley**: a full ball the batter can easily drive as it bounces. Often a gift for the batter.
**Yorker**: pitches right at the batter's toes or the bottom of the stumps. Very hard to dig out.
**Full toss**: reaches the batter without bouncing. Usually easy to hit.
**Beamer**: a full toss that passes above the batter's **waist** (standing upright at the crease). It is dangerous and is called a **no-ball**.
cards.fact: A bowler who bowls dangerous beamers again and again can be taken off by the umpire.

cards.title: The lines
body: **Off stump line**: aimed at the top of off stump. Classic test-match bowling.
**Outside off**: a little wider, tempting the batter to edge it to the keeper or slips.
**Middle** and **leg** lines: attack the stumps and pads, looking for bowled or LBW.
Too far down the leg side is risky: batters can flick it away, and if it's too wide it is a **wide**.

cards.title: The corridor of uncertainty
body: The **corridor of uncertainty** is a narrow line just **outside off stump**.
The batter isn't sure whether to play at it or leave it.
Play at it and you might edge it. Leave it and it might hit the stumps!
Good length plus corridor of uncertainty is a fast bowler's best friend.

cards.title: Why line and length matter
body: A good line and length gives the batter **no easy runs**.
It builds **pressure**, and pressure makes batters take risks.
Bowling to a plan also lets your captain set the **right field**.
Wild bowling is easy to hit and gives away extras.
cards.fact: Many great bowlers say: 'Hit the top of off stump, again and again.'

quiz.q: What does 'length' mean in bowling?
options: How fast the ball is bowled
How far down the pitch the ball bounces
How far the bowler runs in
quiz.ex: Length is where the ball pitches. Line is the side-to-side direction.

quiz.q: Which length makes the batter unsure whether to go forward or back?
quiz.ex: A good length is the hardest to face because the batter can't decide whether to come forward or go back.

quiz.q: A ball pitches right at the batter's toes, at the base of the stumps. What is it called?
quiz.ex: A yorker lands at the batter's feet and is very hard to dig out.

quiz.q: A full toss flies past the batter's chest without bouncing. What does the umpire call?
quiz.ex: A full toss above waist height is a beamer. It is dangerous and is called a no-ball.

quiz.q: What is the 'corridor of uncertainty'?
options: A line just outside off stump
A ball bowled down the leg side
quiz.ex: It's the line just outside off stump where the batter doesn't know whether to play or leave.

quiz.q: Which ball is usually a gift for the batter to drive?
quiz.ex: A half-volley is full enough to be driven easily as it bounces.

quiz.q: A very short ball that rises towards the batter's head is a…
quiz.ex: A bouncer is bowled very short so that it rears up towards the shoulder or head.

quiz.q: True or false: accurate line and length builds pressure and helps take wickets.
quiz.ex: True. Dot balls create pressure, and pressure makes batters take risks.

cards.title: What is pace bowling?
body: Pace bowlers (seamers) rely on **speed** and **movement** to beat the batter.
Top fast bowlers often bowl at **more than 140 km/h**.
Medium-pacers are slower but use swing, seam and accuracy.
Speed alone isn't enough. Control and movement take wickets.

cards.title: Swing bowling
body: **Swing** is when the ball curves **in the air**.
One side of the ball is kept **shiny** and the other gets rough. Fielders polish the shiny side, but **using saliva is not allowed**.
**Conventional swing** moves the ball away from the shiny side.
The **seam** is held upright and pointed the way you want the ball to swing.
cards.fact: For a right-hander, seam pointing towards the slips with the shiny side facing leg gives an out-swinger.

cards.title: In-swing and out-swing
body: **Out-swinger**: curves **away** from the right-hander, towards the slips. It finds edges.
**In-swinger**: curves **into** the right-hander, towards the pads and stumps. It brings bowled and LBW into play.
Mixing both keeps the batter guessing.

cards.title: Reverse swing and seam movement
body: **Reverse swing** happens with an **older**, scuffed ball, often at high pace.
It swings the **opposite way** to conventional swing: towards the shiny side.
**Seam movement** is different: the ball lands on its seam and **moves off the pitch**, not in the air.
Hitting the seam on a green, grassy pitch can make the ball jag sideways.

cards.title: Cutters and slower balls
body: **Cutters** are bowled by rolling the fingers across the seam. An **off-cutter** moves in to the right-hander; a **leg-cutter** moves away.
A **slower ball** looks like a normal delivery but arrives later, so the batter plays too early.
The **knuckle ball** is a slower ball gripped with the knuckles or fingertips so it comes out with very little spin.
Slower balls are hugely useful in T20 cricket.

cards.title: Bouncer and yorker: the big weapons
body: The **bouncer** surprises the batter and pushes them back. Only a limited number per over are allowed in limited-overs cricket.
The **yorker** is aimed at the toes and the base of the stumps. Perfect at the end of an innings.
**Jasprit Bumrah** is famous for his deadly, accurate yorkers.
Using both makes a batter worry about going forward and back.
cards.fact: Fast bowlers wear spikes and warm up properly. Looking after your body is part of bowling fast.

quiz.q: What is 'swing'?
options: The ball spinning off the pitch
The ball curving in the air
quiz.ex: Swing is sideways movement in the air. Movement off the pitch is seam or spin.

quiz.q: An out-swinger to a right-handed batter moves…
quiz.ex: An out-swinger curves away from the right-hander, which can find the edge.

quiz.q: Which type of swing happens with an older, scuffed ball and moves the opposite way to normal swing?
quiz.ex: Reverse swing comes from an old ball and moves towards the shiny side.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT allowed when shining the ball?
quiz.ex: Using saliva on the ball is not allowed under the current laws and playing conditions.

quiz.q: The ball pitches on its seam and suddenly moves sideways off a grassy pitch. This is…
quiz.ex: Seam movement happens off the pitch, after the ball lands on its seam.

quiz.q: A bowler rolls their fingers across the seam and the ball moves into the right-hander. What ball is it?
quiz.ex: An off-cutter moves into the right-handed batter. A leg-cutter moves away.

quiz.q: Which slower ball is gripped with the knuckles or fingertips?
quiz.ex: The knuckle ball comes out with very little spin and arrives slower than the batter expects.

quiz.q: Which bowler is famous for deadly yorkers?
quiz.ex: Jasprit Bumrah's accurate yorkers are feared, especially at the end of an innings.

cards.title: Finger spin and wrist spin
body: Spinners bowl slower and make the ball **turn** after it bounces.
**Finger spinners** spin the ball mainly with their fingers.
**Wrist spinners** flick the ball with their wrist. They can get big turn but it is harder to control.
Remember: all directions here are for a right-handed batter.

cards.title: Off-spin and leg-spin
body: **Off-spin**: right-arm **finger** spin. The ball turns from **off to leg**, into the right-hander.
**Leg-spin**: right-arm **wrist** spin. The ball turns from **leg to off**, away from the right-hander.
**Shane Warne** of Australia was one of the greatest leg-spinners ever.
cards.fact: The off-break and leg-break are named after the side the ball turns FROM.

cards.title: The tricky variations
body: **Googly**: the leg-spinner's surprise. It is bowled with a leg-spin action but turns the **other way**, like an off-break.
**Doosra**: the off-spinner's surprise. It turns the **other way**, from leg to off. **Muttiah Muralitharan** made it famous.
**Top-spinner**: spins forwards, so it dips and bounces more and goes straight on.
**Flipper**: a leg-spinner's ball squeezed out from under the hand. It skids on low and fast.

cards.title: More spinners' tricks
body: **Arm ball**: a finger spinner's ball that doesn't turn but goes straight on with the arm, often catching the batter playing for turn.
**Carrom ball**: flicked out with the middle finger and thumb, like flicking a carrom striker.
Variations work best when they look just like the stock ball.

cards.title: Left-arm spinners
body: **Left-arm orthodox**: left-arm **finger** spin. It turns **away** from the right-hander (leg to off).
**Left-arm wrist spin**: turns **into** the right-hander (off to leg).
**Kuldeep Yadav** of India is a well-known left-arm wrist spinner.

cards.title: Flight, drift, dip and turn
body: **Flight**: tossing the ball up higher and slower to tempt the batter forward.
**Drift**: the spinning ball curving sideways in the air.
**Dip**: the ball dropping sharply, so it lands shorter than the batter expected.
**Turn**: the ball changing direction after it bounces.
cards.fact: Great spinners beat the batter in the air first, with flight, drift and dip, and then off the pitch with turn.

quiz.q: A right-arm off-spinner's stock ball turns which way for a right-handed batter?
options: From leg to off, away from the batter
From off to leg, into the batter
quiz.ex: Off-spin turns from off to leg, into the right-hander.

quiz.q: Leg-spin is which type of spin?
quiz.ex: Leg-spinners use their wrist to spin the ball from leg to off.

quiz.q: A leg-spinner bowls a ball with a leg-spin action, but it turns into the right-hander like an off-break. What is it?
quiz.ex: The googly is the leg-spinner's ball that turns the other way.

quiz.q: Which bowler made the doosra famous?
quiz.ex: Muttiah Muralitharan's doosra turned the other way from his off-breaks.

quiz.q: A finger spinner bowls a ball that doesn't turn but goes straight on with the arm. What is it called?
quiz.ex: The arm ball goes straight on and often catches batters playing for turn.

quiz.q: Left-arm orthodox spin turns which way for a right-hander?
quiz.ex: Left-arm finger spin turns from leg to off, away from the right-hander.

quiz.q: The spinning ball curves sideways in the air before it bounces. This is called…
quiz.ex: Drift is sideways movement in the air. Turn happens after the ball bounces.

quiz.q: Which ball is flicked out with the middle finger and thumb?
quiz.ex: The carrom ball is flicked out like a carrom striker.

cards.title: The maiden over
body: A **maiden over** is an over where the bowler concedes **no runs** against their name.
Byes and leg byes don't spoil a maiden, but a wide, a no-ball or runs off the bat do.
Bowling maidens builds big pressure on the batters.

cards.title: Three key numbers
body: **Economy rate** = runs conceded ÷ overs bowled. Lower is better.
**Bowling average** = runs conceded ÷ wickets taken. Lower is better.
**Bowling strike rate** = balls bowled ÷ wickets taken. It tells you how often a bowler takes a wicket. Lower is better.

cards.title: Worked example
body: A bowler bowls **10 overs**, gives away **40 runs** and takes **2 wickets**.
Economy rate = 40 ÷ 10 = **4.00** runs per over.
Average = 40 ÷ 2 = **20** runs per wicket.
Strike rate = 60 balls ÷ 2 = **30** balls per wicket.
cards.fact: Remember: 10 overs is 60 balls, because each over has 6 legal balls.

cards.title: Hat-tricks and five-fors
body: A **hat-trick** is when a bowler takes wickets with **three consecutive balls**. They can even be spread across two overs.
The wickets must be credited to the bowler, so a run out doesn't count towards a hat-trick.
A **five-wicket haul** (a 'five-for') is taking 5 or more wickets in an innings. It's a huge achievement.

cards.title: Setting up a batter
body: Good bowlers make a **plan**: for example, several balls moving away outside off stump…
…then one that comes back in to hit the pads or stumps.
Or a couple of short balls to push the batter back, then a full one to catch them on the crease.
Watch the batter: do they like driving? Do they struggle with the short ball?

cards.title: Death bowling and bowling to your field
body: The **death overs** are the last overs of a limited-overs innings, when batters try to hit everything.
Death bowlers use **yorkers**, **slower balls** and wide lines to make big hits difficult.
**Bowling to your field** means bowling where your fielders are set. If you have lots of off-side fielders, bowl outside off stump.
If you bowl at the leg side with an off-side field, the batter scores easy runs into the gaps.

quiz.q: A bowler concedes 2 leg byes and nothing else in an over. Is it a maiden?
quiz.ex: Byes and leg byes are not charged to the bowler, so it's still a maiden.

quiz.q: What is the formula for economy rate?
quiz.ex: Economy rate is runs conceded per over.

quiz.q: A bowler takes 3 wickets for 60 runs. What is their bowling average?
quiz.ex: Average = runs ÷ wickets = 60 ÷ 3 = 20.

quiz.q: A bowler takes 2 wickets in 8 overs. What is their strike rate?
quiz.ex: 8 overs = 48 balls. Strike rate = 48 ÷ 2 = 24 balls per wicket.

quiz.q: A bowler gives away 32 runs in 8 overs. What is their economy rate?
quiz.ex: 32 ÷ 8 = 4.00 runs per over.

quiz.q: A bowler takes a wicket with the last ball of one over and the first two balls of their next over. Is it a hat-trick?
options: No, it must be in one over
quiz.ex: A hat-trick is three wickets in three consecutive balls by the same bowler, even across overs.

quiz.q: What is a 'five-for'?
options: Five or more wickets in an innings
quiz.ex: A five-wicket haul is 5 or more wickets in one innings.

quiz.q: Your captain has set a field with most fielders on the off side. Where should you bowl?
quiz.ex: Bowling to your field means bowling where your fielders can stop the ball, here on the off side.

modules.title: Fielding and Wicket-keeping
modules.desc: Catch, stop, throw, keep wicket and think like a captain.

cards.title: Catches win matches
body: Dropping a catch gives a good batter another chance, and they might score many more runs.
The two golden rules: **watch the ball** all the way into your hands, and use **soft hands**.
**Soft hands** means letting your hands give, moving back with the ball as it arrives, like catching an egg.
cards.fact: Every fielder, even the best batter in the team, needs to be a good catcher.

cards.title: High catches
body: Get under the ball early and keep your **eyes on it**.
Use the **reverse cup**: hands up near your face, **fingers pointing up**, thumbs together.
Or the **basket** style: hands low near your chest, fingers pointing forward, little fingers together.
Call **'Mine!'** loudly so teammates don't crash into you.

cards.title: Slip catching
body: Slip fielders stand in a **low**, balanced crouch, weight on the balls of their feet.
Stay **still** as the bowler bowls. Watch the edge of the bat.
**Let the ball come** to you. Don't snatch at it, and keep your fingers pointing down for low catches.
Slip catches come very fast, so practise with a coach or a catching cradle.

cards.title: When is a catch completed?
body: A catch is completed when the fielder has **complete control** over the **ball** and over their **own movement**.
If you catch it and then drop it as you fall over, it is **not out**.
The ball must not touch the ground before it is caught.
A ball caught off the batter's glove (while it's touching the bat) counts as caught too.

cards.title: Boundary catches
body: When you touch the ball, you must **not be touching the boundary rope** or the ground beyond it. If you are, it's a **six**.
You may **jump from inside** the boundary and, while in the **air**, knock the ball back into the field.
You or a teammate can then complete the catch inside the field.
Practise this with friends: it's a skill top fielders use all the time.
cards.fact: Keep your eyes on the rope as well as the ball. Many great catches are ruined by a foot on the boundary.

quiz.q: What does 'soft hands' mean when catching?
options: Letting your hands give as the ball arrives
quiz.ex: Soft hands means moving your hands back with the ball so it doesn't bounce out.

quiz.q: For a high catch using the reverse cup, your fingers should point…
quiz.ex: In the reverse cup, hands are up near the face with fingers pointing up.

quiz.q: What should you shout when going for a high catch?
quiz.ex: Calling 'Mine!' stops teammates colliding with you.

quiz.q: How should a slip fielder wait for the ball?
quiz.ex: Slip fielders crouch low, stay still and let the ball come to them.

quiz.q: A fielder catches the ball, then falls and the ball pops out as they hit the ground. Is it out?
options: Only if the umpire saw it
quiz.ex: A catch needs complete control of the ball and of your own movement. Dropping it while falling means not out.

quiz.q: A fielder catches the ball with one foot touching the boundary rope. What is it?
quiz.ex: Touching the rope while touching the ball means the ball is over the boundary. It's six.

quiz.q: A fielder jumps from inside the boundary, knocks the ball back into the field while in the air, then lands and a teammate catches it. Is it out?
quiz.ex: That's allowed: they jumped from inside and knocked the ball back while airborne, and the catch was completed inside the field.

quiz.q: True or false: the ball must not touch the ground before a catch is completed.
quiz.ex: True. If it bounces first, it's not a catch.

cards.title: Attack the ball
body: Good fielders **walk in** as the bowler bowls, so they're moving and ready.
**Attack the ball**: run towards it, don't wait for it to come to you.
Every run you save counts. Matches are often won by just a few runs!

cards.title: The long barrier
body: The **long barrier** is the safest way to stop a ball, especially on a bumpy outfield.
Turn side-on and go down on one knee so your knee meets the other foot's heel, making a **wall** with your legs.
Hands together in front, fingers pointing down.
If the ball misses your hands, your body still stops it.

cards.title: Quick pick-ups
body: The **one-handed pick-up** is faster, used when you need to stop a run quickly.
Get your body low and pick the ball up beside your front foot.
The **sliding stop** saves runs near the boundary: slide down, stop the ball, and get up fast to throw.
On the boundary, two fielders can work together: one stops it, the other throws.

cards.title: Throwing
body: Use a **crow hop**: a little skip towards your target that puts power into the throw.
Point your front shoulder and non-throwing arm at the target.
Throw **flat and hard** to the keeper or bowler, aiming just above the stumps.
Long throws from the deep can use a **relay**: throw to a teammate in between, who throws on.
cards.fact: A flat throw reaching the keeper on one bounce is often quicker and easier to take than a big, looping full toss.

cards.title: Direct hits and backing up
body: A **direct hit** on the stumps can run out a batter.
But if you miss, the ball can run away for **overthrows**.
So other fielders must **back up**: stand behind the stumps in line with the throw to stop it running away.
The bowler often backs up at their end.

quiz.q: What should a fielder do as the bowler runs in?
quiz.ex: Walking in means you are moving and ready to attack the ball.

quiz.q: Which technique makes a wall with your legs to stop the ball safely?
quiz.ex: The long barrier puts your body behind the ball so it can't get past.

quiz.q: What is a crow hop?
options: A skip towards your target to power your throw
quiz.ex: The crow hop builds momentum towards your target for a stronger throw.

quiz.q: Where should you aim a throw to the keeper?
options: Flat and just above the stumps
quiz.ex: A flat throw just above the stumps lets the keeper break the wicket quickly.

quiz.q: Why do fielders back up a throw?
options: To stop overthrows if the throw misses
quiz.ex: Backing up stops the ball running away for extra runs if the throw misses.

quiz.q: The ball is hit far into the deep. A fielder throws it to a teammate in between, who throws it on to the keeper. This is a…
quiz.ex: A relay throw is used when the throw is too long for one fielder.

quiz.q: Which pick-up is faster but riskier?
quiz.ex: The one-handed pick-up saves time but the ball can slip past if you miss it.

quiz.q: A fielder chases the ball to the boundary and slides to stop it just before the rope. What is this called?
quiz.ex: The sliding stop is a quick way to stop the ball near the boundary and save runs.

cards.title: The keeper's job
body: The **wicket-keeper** stands behind the stumps at the batter's end.
They are the **only fielder** allowed to wear **gloves** and **external leg guards** (pads).
Keepers take the ball when the batter misses it, catch edges, do **stumpings** and take throws for run outs.
cards.fact: The keeper touches the ball more than anyone else on the field.

cards.title: The stance
body: Keepers start in a **squat**: low down, weight on the balls of the feet, gloves together and resting low.
Stay down until the ball bounces, then rise with it.
Keep your head still and watch the ball all the way.

cards.title: Standing back and standing up
body: For **fast bowlers**, keepers **stand back**, often many metres behind the stumps, to have time to take the ball.
For **spinners**, keepers **stand up** close to the stumps, ready for a stumping.
Sometimes keepers stand up to medium-pacers too, to stop batters walking down the pitch.

cards.title: Stumpings and catches
body: **Stumped**: the batter is out of their crease (not trying a run) and the keeper breaks the wicket with the ball.
A batter can even be **stumped off a wide**, but not off a no-ball.
Edges that fly behind are **caught behind** by the keeper.
Take the ball cleanly with **soft hands**, fingers pointing down or sideways, never straight at the ball.

cards.title: Don't take it in front!
body: The keeper must **not take the ball in front of the stumps** before it has passed the wicket or touched the bat or batter.
If they do, it is a **no-ball**, and any stumping doesn't count.
So keepers wait patiently behind the stumps.

cards.title: The leader behind the stumps
body: The keeper has the best view of the game.
They **talk to the fielders**, encourage the bowlers and help the captain with field placements.
They call **'Bowler!'** or **'Keeper!'** to say which end a throw should go to.
A good keeper keeps the team's energy up all day.

quiz.q: Which fielder is allowed to wear gloves?
quiz.ex: Only the wicket-keeper may wear gloves and external leg guards.

quiz.q: What is the wicket-keeper's starting stance?
quiz.ex: Keepers start low in a squat and rise with the ball.

quiz.q: A fast bowler is bowling. Where does the keeper usually stand?
quiz.ex: Keepers stand back for fast bowlers so they have time to take the ball.

quiz.q: A spinner is bowling. Why does the keeper stand up to the stumps?
quiz.ex: Standing up lets the keeper stump a batter who leaves the crease.

quiz.q: The batter leaves the crease to a wide, misses, and the keeper breaks the wicket. Is it out?
options: No, you can't be out off a wide
Only if the batter was running
quiz.ex: A batter can be stumped off a wide, but not off a no-ball.

quiz.q: The keeper reaches in front of the stumps and grabs the ball before it reaches the wicket. What does the umpire call?
quiz.ex: The keeper must not take the ball in front of the stumps before it passes the wicket or touches the bat or batter.

quiz.q: An edge flies behind and the keeper catches it. How is the batter out?
quiz.ex: That's caught, often called 'caught behind'.

quiz.q: True or false: the keeper should help lead and encourage the fielders.
quiz.ex: True. The keeper has the best view and is often the team's voice on the field.

cards.title: The toss
body: Before the match the captains **toss a coin**. The winner chooses to **bat** or **bowl** first.
Look at the **pitch**: a dry, cracked pitch may help spinners later, so batting first can be good.
Look at the **sky**: cloudy, damp conditions often help swing bowlers, so bowling first can be good.
In limited-overs games, some captains prefer to **chase** so they know the target.

cards.title: Batting order
body: **Openers** face the new ball. They need good technique and patience.
The best batters often bat at **3 and 4**.
Big hitters and all-rounders often come in the **middle and lower order** to finish an innings.
Captains can change the order depending on the situation.

cards.title: Bowling changes
body: Start with your best **new-ball bowlers** when the ball is shiny and hard.
Bring on **spinners** when the ball gets older or the pitch starts to turn.
Keep short **spells** for fast bowlers so they stay fresh.
Change the bowler if a batter gets comfortable. A new face can break a partnership.

cards.title: Field placements
body: **Attacking field**: slips, gully and close catchers to take wickets.
**Defensive field**: fielders spread out to stop runs and boundaries.
Set the field to match the bowler's plan and the batter's favourite shots.
Always follow the fielding restrictions, like the powerplay rules.

cards.title: Using reviews wisely
body: In matches with the **Decision Review System (DRS)**, teams can challenge an umpire's decision.
Each team has only a **limited number** of unsuccessful reviews, so don't waste them.
Listen to the bowler and keeper, but think: was it really out? Save reviews for clear mistakes.

cards.title: The Spirit of Cricket
body: Cricket is played in the **Spirit of Cricket**: respect for your **opponents**, **teammates**, the **umpires** and the game.
Accept the umpire's decision without arguing.
Clap a good shot or a great catch, even from the other team.
Shake hands at the end. Play hard, but play fair.
cards.fact: The Laws of Cricket begin with a Preamble about the Spirit of Cricket. That's how important it is!

quiz.q: Who chooses whether to bat or bowl first?
options: The captain who wins the toss
quiz.ex: The captain who wins the toss decides to bat or bowl.

quiz.q: It's cloudy and damp, and the ball is likely to swing. What might a captain choose after winning the toss?
quiz.ex: Swing-friendly conditions often make bowling first a good choice.

quiz.q: When are spinners usually brought on?
options: When the ball is older or the pitch starts to turn
quiz.ex: Spinners usually do best once the shine has gone and the pitch is helping turn.

quiz.q: A field with three slips, a gully and a short leg is…
quiz.ex: Lots of close catchers means the captain is trying to take wickets.

quiz.q: Which fielding setup is mainly for stopping runs?
options: Fielders spread out in the deep
Close catchers all round the bat
quiz.ex: A defensive field spreads fielders out to stop boundaries.

quiz.q: Why should a team use reviews carefully?
options: Each team has a limited number of unsuccessful reviews
quiz.ex: If you waste your reviews, you may not have one when a real mistake happens.

quiz.q: The umpire gives you out and you think it was wrong. With no review left, what should you do?
quiz.ex: The Spirit of Cricket means respecting the umpire's decision.

quiz.q: True or false: clapping a great catch by the other team is part of the Spirit of Cricket.
quiz.ex: True. Respecting your opponents is a big part of the game.

quiz.q: How long is a cricket pitch, from stumps to stumps?
quiz.ex: The pitch is 22 yards (20.12 m) long.

quiz.q: How many ways of being out are there in the Laws (not counting retired out)?
quiz.ex: Bowled, caught, hit the ball twice, hit wicket, LBW, obstructing the field, run out, stumped and timed out: 9.

quiz.q: The ball pitches outside leg stump and would have hit the stumps. The batter is hit on the pad. Can it be LBW?
options: Yes, if it would hit the stumps
Only if no shot was played
quiz.ex: A ball that pitches outside leg stump can never be LBW.

quiz.q: In an ODI, the bowler oversteps the popping crease. What happens next ball?
quiz.ex: Every no-ball in ODIs and T20Is is followed by a free hit.

quiz.q: On a free hit, the batter is bowled. Is the batter out?
quiz.ex: On a free hit you can only be out in ways possible off a no-ball, such as run out. Bowled isn't one of them.

quiz.q: The umpire raises both arms straight above their head. What does it mean?
quiz.ex: Both arms raised above the head signals six. Waving one arm across the body is four.

quiz.q: In a T20I powerplay (first 6 overs), how many fielders may be outside the 30-yard circle?
quiz.ex: During the T20I powerplay only 2 fielders are allowed outside the circle.

quiz.q: A batter is caught. The batters had crossed before the catch, and it isn't the last ball of the over. Who faces the next ball?
quiz.ex: Since 2022, the new batter always takes strike after a catch (unless it was the end of the over).

quiz.q: The bowler runs out the non-striker who left the crease before the ball was bowled. How is the batter out?
quiz.ex: Since the 2022 law change, this is simply run out under Law 38.

quiz.q: Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Gully is behind point, in an attacking catching position on the off side.

quiz.q: Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Third man is near the boundary behind the batter on the off side.

quiz.q: Which fielding position is marked?
quiz.ex: Mid-wicket is on the leg side, between square leg and mid-on.

quiz.q: Which close catching position is marked?
quiz.ex: Silly point is very close to the batter on the off side, square of the wicket.

quiz.q: A right-hander hits a short ball hard along the arrow, square on the leg side. Which shot is it most likely to be?
quiz.ex: The pull shot sends a short ball square on the leg side, towards square leg or mid-wicket.

quiz.q: A right-hander leans forward and hits a full ball along the arrow through the off side. Which shot is it?
quiz.ex: The cover drive is played on the front foot to a full ball and goes through the covers.

quiz.q: A ball curves away from the right-hander in the air towards the slips. It is…
quiz.ex: An out-swinger swings away from the right-handed batter.

quiz.q: A leg-spinner bowls a ball that turns into the right-hander, the opposite of a leg-break. What is it?
quiz.ex: The googly turns like an off-break, though it's bowled with a leg-spin action.

quiz.q: A bowler takes 4 wickets for 36 runs in 9 overs. What is the bowling average?
quiz.ex: Average = runs ÷ wickets = 36 ÷ 4 = 9. (Economy rate would be 36 ÷ 9 = 4.00.)

quiz.q: What is the maximum elbow extension the ICC allows in a bowling action?
quiz.ex: More than 15 degrees of elbow straightening is illegal.

quiz.q: The ball hits a fielder's helmet that has been left on the ground behind the keeper. What happens?
options: 5 penalty runs to the batting side
quiz.ex: Hitting a fielder's helmet on the ground gives the batting side 5 penalty runs.

quiz.q: A fielder catches the ball near the rope but, while holding it, steps on the boundary. What is the result?
quiz.ex: A fielder touching the ball while touching the boundary means the ball is over the boundary, so it's six.

quiz.q: The batter dances down the pitch to a spinner, misses, and the keeper whips off the bails. The ball was a no-ball. Is the batter stumped?
quiz.ex: You cannot be stumped off a no-ball (though you can be off a wide).

quiz.q: Who was the first batter to be timed out in men's international cricket?
quiz.ex: Angelo Mathews of Sri Lanka was timed out against Bangladesh at the 2023 World Cup.

quiz.q: A delivery is called a beamer. What makes it a beamer?
options: It pitches at the batter's toes
It's a full toss above the batter's waist
quiz.ex: A full toss passing above waist height is a dangerous beamer and is called a no-ball.

quiz.q: Under Law 28.4, how many fielders (not counting the keeper) may be behind square on the leg side when the ball is bowled?
quiz.ex: No more than 2 fielders may be behind the popping crease on the leg side at the moment of delivery.
